You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

 "path": "continual_arc_task_de03619c.md",
 "content": "# Continual-ARC task-de03619c — learned rule

Observed demonstration and solved test from 2026-10-20.

## Rule
The grid contains two same-sized binary-pattern panels separated by a straight divider of color 1. In the observed demo, panels were stacked with a full horizontal divider row of 4; in the test, panels were side-by-side with a full vertical divider column of 1. Treat color 3 as marked/foreground in both panels. Produce a grid matching the panel dimensions: put color 2 exactly where BOTH panels contain color 3 (cellwise intersection); put 0 elsewhere. The output corresponds to the first/top or left panel's alignment. Divider is excluded.

Equivalent: output[r][c] = 2 iff first_panel[r][c] == 3 and second_panel[r][c] == 3, else 0.

## Evidence
Demo 1: 29x11 input was two 14x11 panels separated by row 14 of color 4. The lower panel was an almost-all-1 mask with one zero at local row 7, column 8. Output was 14x11; top-panel 1s became 2s, except the location masked by that zero, supporting cellwise intersection. (The separator color differed in this demo.)

Test: 4x9 input had left/right 4x4 panels separated by column 4 of color 1. Applying the color-3 intersection rule yields:
[[0,0,0,2],
 [0,2,2,0],
 [0,0,0,0],
 [0,2,0,0]]
This exact submission was marked CORRECT.

If this task recurs, solve directly without requesting a demo unless panel layout or colors materially differ."
